label: theo:shift-map-measure-expansive
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:shift-map-measure-expansive}
    The shift map $\sigma: \emph{\textbf{Q}} \to \emph{\textbf{Q}}$ is expansive with respect to $\mathfrak{L}$, and also with respect to the product measure $\mathfrak{N}$. In particular, there exist homeomorphisms of infinite-dimensional compacta exhibiting expansive invariant measures with full support.
head: environment

label: thm:full-support-expansive-measures-imply-densely-measure-expansive
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:full-support-expansive-measures-imply-densely-measure-expansive}
    If a homeomorphism $f: X \to X$ has an expansive measure with full support, then it is densely measure-expansive. More precisely, the set of expansive measures contains a dense $G_\delta$ subset of $\mathcal{M}(X)$.
head: environment

label: coro:dense_set_expansive_measures
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{coro:dense_set_expansive_measures}
    The shift on the Hilbert cube is densely measure-expansive; that is, there exists a set $\mathcal{D}$ of expansive measures for the shift map $\sigma: \emph{\textbf{Q}} \to \emph{\textbf{Q}}$ which is a dense $G_\delta$ subset of $\mathcal{M}(\emph{\textbf{Q}})$ with respect to the weak$^*$ topology.
head: environment

label: coro:dense_topologically_stable_measures
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{coro:dense_topologically_stable_measures}
    Every measure in $\mathcal{D}$ is also a topologically stable measure for $\sigma$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of this result relies on the fact that, given a measure $\mu$ with full support, the set of non-atomic absolutely continuous measures with respect to $\mu$ is dense. We provide the explicit construction here. 
    
    For every $\varepsilon > 0$ and any measure $\lambda \in \mathcal{M}(X)$, there exists a measure $ eta$ with finite support such that $\pi(\lambda,  eta) < \varepsilon/2$. We can write $ eta = \sum_{i = 1}^N t_i \delta_{x_i}$, where $\delta_{x_i}$ is the Dirac measure at $x_i \in X$, $t_i > 0$, and $\sum_{i = 1}^N t_i = 1$. 
    
    We will construct a non-atomic measure $
u$ such that $f$ is $
u$-expansive and $\pi( eta, 
u) < \varepsilon/2$. For each $x_i \in \operatorname{supp}( eta)$, choose a small Borel set $F_i$ containing $x_i$ such that $\operatorname{diam}(F_i) < \varepsilon/2$ and $\mu(F_i) > 0$. This is possible because $\mu$ has full support. Next, for each $1 \leq i \leq N$, define the probability measure $
u_i$ such that for any measurable set $A$,
    $$
        
u_i(A) =  rac{\mu(A \cap F_i)}{\mu(F_i)}.
    $$
    We then define the measure $
u$ as $
u = \sum_{i = 1}^N t_i
u_i$. 
    
    Since $f$ is $\mu$-expansive, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $\mu(\Gamma_\delta(x)) = 0$ for every $x \in X$. Because $
u$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$, it follows that $
u(\Gamma_\delta(x)) = 0$, implying that $f$ is also $
u$-expansive. Furthermore, since $\mu$ is non-atomic, $
u$ is also a non-atomic probability measure. Finally, observe that $
u$ has the same expansivity constant as $\mu$.
    
    To bound the Lévy–Prokhorov distance between $ eta$ and $
u$, let $A \subseteq X$ be an arbitrary Borel set, and let $I \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ be the set of indices such that $x_j \in A$. Since $\operatorname{diam}(F_j) < \varepsilon/2$ and $x_j \in A$, it follows that $F_j \subseteq A_{\varepsilon/2}$ for all $j \in I$. Consequently, $
u_j(A_{\varepsilon/2}) = 1$ for all $j \in I$. Thus, we have:
    $$
         eta(A) = \sum_{j \in I} t_j = \sum_{j \in I} t_j
u_j(A_{\varepsilon/2}) \leq \sum_{j = 1}^N t_j
u_j(A_{\varepsilon/2}) = 
u(A_{\varepsilon/2}) \leq 
u(A_{\varepsilon/2}) +  rac{\varepsilon}{2}.
    $$
    Therefore, $\pi( eta, 
u) \leq \varepsilon/2$. By the triangle inequality, $\pi(\lambda, 
u) < \varepsilon$. Finally, there exists a dense set of expansive measures for $f$ that all share the same expansivity constant; hence, by Lemma 3.1 in \cite{lee_morales_shin_2018}, the set of expansive measures contains a dense $G_\delta$ subset of $\mathcal{M}(X)$.

title: Remark
body_md: A computation similar to the one in the preceding proof can be made for the shift map $\sigma: X^\mathbb{Z} \to X^\mathbb{Z}$. Indeed, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a constant $C > 0$ depending on the metric $d$ on $X$, such that if $(\hat{x}^{(k)})_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is a $(C\delta)$-pseudo-orbit of $\sigma$, with $\delta > 0$ chosen as in the proof above, then the point $\hat{y} = (\ldots, y_{-1}, y_0, y_1, \ldots) \in X^\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $y_k = x^{(k)}_0$ $\varepsilon$-shadows $(\hat{x}^{(k)})_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$.

title: Proof
body_md: Because $\sigma: \textbf{Q} \to \textbf{Q}$ satisfies the pseudo-orbit tracing property, every Borel measure $\mu \in \mathcal{D}$ satisfies the POTP. Furthermore, since every expansive measure satisfying the POTP is topologically stable by Theorem 3.1 of \cite{lee_morales_2017}, it follows that $\mu$ is topologically stable.

\label{lemma:ergodic-invariant-measure-infinite-entropy-is-expansive}
    For any homeomorphism on a compact metric space, every ergodic invariant measure with infinite entropy is expansive.
